name: Accessibility in Every Classroom
title: Accessibility in Every Classroom
answer: Accessibility in every classroom means making tools such as live captions, text to speech, dictation, and image descriptions available to all students, not only those with disabilities. This helps students who need them avoid standing out while also supporting English learners, students in noisy rooms, and others. It matters because accessible materials and plain language do not happen automatically, so teachers must decide when a support opens access and when it might replace the skill a lesson is teaching.

sections.body: The idea is that many accessibility supports are useful far beyond the students who qualify for them. Live captions in Microsoft PowerPoint and Teams serve students who are deaf or hard of hearing, and they also help English learners and students in noisy rooms. Text to speech and dictation through Microsoft Immersive Reader or Read&Write by Texthelp serve students with reading or writing disabilities and many others. When these tools are available to everyone, students who need them do not have to stand out. The problem it solves is both practical and social: it removes access barriers while reducing the stigma of using a support, and it raises the question of when a support should be used so that a student still builds the skills the lesson targets.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, live captions can run during presentations and meetings, and text to speech or dictation can be available through Microsoft Immersive Reader or Read&Write by Texthelp. Image descriptions open visual content for students who are blind or have low vision, using tools such as Microsoft Seeing AI, which is free, or Be My Eyes, which requires users to be at least 17 and so suits staff and older students only. Teachers can write alternative text for images in their own materials, with AI helping to draft descriptions that the teacher then checks. For a student with dyslexia, text to speech in history class opens the content, while in a reading lesson the IEP team decides whether and how the student should use it. Simplified directions and texts help many students, but teachers may need to prompt AI specifically for plain language and check the results.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book does not give an evidence label for this idea. It cites researchers who describe strategic offloading, where a tool handles the part of a task that blocks access while the student still builds the skills the lesson targets (Seung & Basham, 2026). It also cites a study of quiz questions generated by AI for students who are deaf or hard of hearing that found frequent compound sentences, double negatives, and complex clauses (Chen et al., 2026). Teachers had to prompt specifically for plain language and check the results, and the text concludes that accessible does not happen automatically.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are that AI output can be complex by default, as the study of quiz questions shows, so teachers must check and prompt for plain language. Image descriptions drafted by AI also need teacher review before use. Some tools carry their own limits, such as Be My Eyes requiring users to be at least 17. Decisions stay with people: the IEP team decides whether and how a student with dyslexia uses text to speech in a reading lesson, and teachers decide when a support is strategic offloading rather than a replacement for the targeted skill. Accessible materials are not automatic, so the responsibility for checking and choosing remains with staff.
